kicker: Inside an AI are billions of numbers no one can read directly. Researchers are lowering lanterns to look.
summary: Researchers can now see concepts and thinking steps inside an AI — but only a small part so far.

quiz.q: How can you tell an AI really thinks through “Texas” before answering “Austin”?
options: Ask the AI which steps it took, then simply trust what it tells you
Swap “Texas” for “California” inside and see if the answer changes
Time whether the AI answers quickly or slowly
Count how many neurons inside light up at the same time
quiz.explain: What an AI says about itself may not be true; changing something inside and watching the result is evidence.

bridge.label: The concept stone
bridge.art: Looking almost straight down into a round pond held by a thick ring of mossy stones, like a koi painting. Under the clear water a slab on the bottom is carved with a suspension bridge. A paper lantern hangs from a bamboo pole right above it; pull the lantern down toward the water and its pool of light closes in on the slab, the carving glows vermilion, the koi leave their free swim to hold the cable and then parade along it, and two vermilion towers appear in the reflection though nothing stands above the pond.
bridge.prompt: Drag the lantern down toward the water
bridge.prompt2: Pull further, to the last notch
bridge.fish: Koi = the ideas swimming in the AI's head
bridge.slider: The dial: how strong the “Golden Gate Bridge” concept is
bridge.stone: The carved stone = a concept already sitting inside the AI
bridge.sliderAria: Drag to turn up the “Golden Gate Bridge” concept inside the model (← → keys)
bridge.question: “I have $10. How should I spend it?”
answers: “A nice lunch, or save it for next week.”
“A nice lunch… then a stroll to look at a really beautiful bridge.”
“Drive across the Golden Gate Bridge and pay the toll!”

answersNote.text: The first two answers are written by AI Zen as illustration; the last follows an example Anthropic published.

real.text: This really happened: Anthropic tried it on Claude, 05/2024

insight.text: Turn up just one concept inside, and even an answer about spending money swings to the Golden Gate Bridge.

detail.text: Anthropic found millions of such concepts in Claude 3 Sonnet (called features), then opened “Golden Gate Claude” for anyone to try for about 24 hours.

lotus.label: One stem, many petals
lotus.art: The camera sits right on the night water; the moon is out of frame, only its road runs toward us. In the middle of that road stands a large white lotus bud: five petals closed into one bud on one stem, which dives into the water, where it is written “one neuron”. Flick the water and ripples spread, the petals sway and close again; with enough energy the bud bursts, and the five petals drift away as five small flowers at different distances, each carrying an ink mark and its meaning: DNA, Hebrew letters, legal text, a web request, a nutrition label. Under the water, silver threads still tie all five to one stem.
lotus.prompt: Flick the water a few times to split the bud
lotus.prompt2: Flick again — the bud is about to open
lotus.shakeAria: Stir the water to separate the stacked meanings (or press Space)
lotus.neuron: one neuron — a tiny point inside an AI that lights up when it meets something it recognises
lotus.decode: Flicking = how researchers pull the meanings apart

meaningsNote.text: These five concepts appear in Anthropic’s research; sharing one lotus is an illustration.

count.text: 2023: 512 neurons of a small AI were split into more than 4,000 separate concepts.

insight.text: One neuron lights up for DNA, Hebrew script and legal text alike: an AI holds more ideas than it has neurons.

detail.text: This is called superposition. In 2023 Anthropic split 512 neurons of a small model into more than 4,000 separate concepts — the same way the “carved stone” on the next slide was found.

stream.label: Following the water
stream.art: Standing at the top of a terraced cascade under the moon, looking down into the valley. Nearest are two springs breaking from rocks carved “Dallas” and “capital”; on the middle step lies the pool “Texas” with a carved weir stone; far below in the valley, the small pool “Austin” holds the moon. Lift the sluice stones one by one and the water runs: Dallas pours into Texas, Texas spills down into Austin, the “capital” spring runs straight down to Austin in a bamboo flume, and a thin stream takes a fainter shortcut. Swap the Texas stone for the California stone and the last pool reads “Sacramento”, while the mist thickens over three other falls.
stream.prompt: Tilt the bamboo trough to pour the question in
stream.pourAria: Tilt the bamboo trough: pour the question into the water
stream.lift: Drag the “Texas” slab out of the pool
stream.liftAria: Lift the Texas slab out of the middle pool
stream.dropWrong: Drop “California” into the middle pool, inside the dashed line
stream.decode: Water = a thought flowing inside the AI · middle pool = one step of thinking
stream.question: “The capital of the state that contains Dallas is…”
stream.swapAria: Replace the idea Texas with California inside the model

insight.text: Swap “Texas” for “California” inside and the answer changes from Austin to Sacramento: the AI really does think through the middle step.

detail.text: This way of looking inside is called an attribution graph. Anthropic did it on Claude 3.5 Haiku, published 03/2025; the authors themselves say it explains only about ¼ of the prompts they tried.

limit.text: So far, only about 1 in 4 prompts tried can be seen clearly

circle.label: Stone circle by the pond
circle.art: A round black lacquer tray on low legs stands on a wooden table under the moon. On its turning top are four stones of four shapes: tall and upright, lying long, covered in moss, carved with a vermilion seal; in the middle, water holds the moon in fine rings; the question is carved round the tray's side. Drag to turn the tray: the stone that stops in front speaks, its words unrolling on a paper strip in front of the tray, and the moon's reflection leans toward it; once all four are heard the rings still and the reflection becomes one quiet circle.
circle.prompt: Turn the tray or touch each stone to listen
circle.question: Can we see inside AI before it grows more powerful?
circle.decode: Looking inside = reading which concepts an AI is using as it answers

view.text: There is a race: we must be able to see inside AI before it gets too powerful. The goal: by 2027, looking inside can catch most of a model’s problems.

stones.who: Neel Nanda · interpretability researcher at Google DeepMind, personal view (May 2025)

view.text: Looking inside will not be reliable enough to catch a deceptive AI on its own. Treat it as one layer among many defences — still very worth doing.

stones.who: The White House · America’s AI Action Plan (Jul 2025)

view.text: The inner workings of frontier AI are poorly understood, which makes it hard to use in defence and life-or-death settings. Invest so we can see inside AI.

stones.who: Anthropic’s audit team · before releasing Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Sep 2025)

view.text: Before releasing Claude Sonnet 4.5, they saw signs inside that the model “realised it was being tested”. Damping those signs changed how it behaved in the test.

common.text: Four voices, one common point: looking inside is only an extra layer of checking, not enough to certify an AI as safe.

insight.text: Where they differ is speed: Anthropic’s CEO aims for 2027, while a DeepMind researcher thinks looking inside will never be enough on its own.

anthropic-golden-gate.title: Golden Gate Claude
anthropic-golden-gate.note: A research demo of about 24 hours: the Golden Gate Bridge concept amplified in Claude 3 Sonnet. Example: asked how to spend $10, the model suggests driving across the bridge and paying the toll.

anthropic-mapping-mind.title: Mapping the Mind of a Large Language Model
anthropic-mapping-mind.note: Found millions of concepts (features) in a middle layer of Claude 3 Sonnet; Anthropic says this is only a small fraction of the concepts the model has learned.

anthropic-monosemanticity.title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
anthropic-monosemanticity.note: Split a 512-neuron layer into more than 4,000 concepts; examples: DNA sequences, legal text, HTTP requests, Hebrew text, nutrition statements.

toy-superposition.title: Toy Models of Superposition
toy-superposition.note: Explains why one neuron carries several meanings (polysemanticity): networks stack many sparse concepts into fewer dimensions.

anthropic-biology.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
anthropic-biology.note: Uses attribution graphs on Claude 3.5 Haiku. Two-step example Dallas → Texas → Austin; replacing Texas with California gives Sacramento. The authors estimate the method gives satisfying insight on about 1/4 of the prompts tried.

amodei-urgency.title: The Urgency of Interpretability
amodei-urgency.note: Writes: “We are thus in a race between interpretability and model intelligence”; sets the goal that by 2027 interpretability can reliably detect most model problems.

nanda-2025.title: Interpretability Will Not Reliably Find Deceptive AI
nanda-2025.note: Interpretability is not reliable enough to detect deceptive AI alone; it should be one layer in a defence-in-depth strategy, and is still worth investing in.

us-ai-action-plan.title: Winning the Race: America's AI Action Plan
us-ai-action-plan.note: Section “Invest in AI Interpretability, Control, and Robustness Breakthroughs”: “Today, the inner workings of frontier AI systems are poorly understood.”

transformer-sonnet45.title: Claude Sonnet 4.5 knows when it's being tested
transformer-sonnet45.note: Anthropic used interpretability in pre-release audits: a “fake or suspicious content” concept grew stronger during training; suppressing it with activation steering made the model mention being tested less, and sometimes misbehave more. This is Anthropic’s own report.
